tweets.text:
Ramtin on how investors justify paying billion-dollar entry prices

"Every few years in Silicon Valley, the goalpost moves for what terminal outcomes can be. 

When I got started in early-stage investing in 2016, people looked at every company through the lens of, 'In a best-case scenario, this could be a $10 billion outcome,' and priced deals accordingly. 

Then you got towards 2021, and everybody started looking at companies through the lens of, 'In a best-case scenario, this company can be worth $100 billion.'

And now we're at a new goalpost of, 'In a best-case scenario, this company could have a trillion-dollar outcome.' 

My bet is there might be two to three more, and not 40 more. 

But now everyone's looking at companies through the lens of, 'In a best-case scenario, you have a trillion-dollar outcome, so what is a $1 billion entry valuation in a trillion-dollar outcome scenario?'"

tweets.text:
BREAKING: Global crude oil in transit is up to 1.28 billion barrels, an all-time high.

This figure has surged +180 million barrels over the last several weeks.

This comes as Middle Eastern oil flows recover through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, while more crude remains at sea for longer.

Ship-to-ship transfers are keeping oil aboard tankers for longer, while extended shipping routes are increasing transit times.

Meanwhile, global oil importers diversifying away from the Middle East are lengthening voyages, leaving more crude tied up aboard tankers.

As a result, more oil remains in transit rather than being readily available to refiners, tightening near-term supply despite recovering export flows.

Oil is flowing, but timely delivery is becoming the bottleneck.

tweets.text:
John Somorjai of Salesforce on the exit math behind today's startup valuations, and a16z's Alex Immerman on the much bigger outcomes that now drive returns:

John: "I think there's a lot of irresponsibility going on. The valuations are of course way too high."

"When you think about investing, you want to think about, what are my exit opportunities? And not every company is going to go public. In fact, very, very few companies go public, probably 1% or less."

"Once you get above $10 billion, for example, the buyer universe is so small, and yet you're seeing so many of these enormous multi-billion dollar valued companies out there, and there will be a reckoning that happens."

"A lot of these companies have valuations that are not sustainable, that they won't be able to grow into, and are also, I think, going to be bad for their employees."

Alex: "Part of my optimism comes from what a top one percent outcome was 10 years ago is very different from what a top one percent outcome is today... There have been these larger outcomes that drive the returns for the ecosystem at large."

John: "I'm an optimist. I could not do my job if I wasn't an optimist. But just know that I see the thousands of companies every year that don't make it. Because they all come to us to try to be acquired."

@jsomorjai @aleximm

"A lot of these companies have valuations that are not sustainable, that they won't be able to grow into, and are also, I think, going to be bad for their employees."

Alex: "Part of my optimism comes from what a top one percent outcome was 10 years ago is very different from what a top one percent outcome is today... There have been these larger outcomes that drive the returns for the ecosystem at large."

John: "I'm an optimist. I could not do my job if I wasn't an optimist. But just know that I see the thousands of companies every year that don't make it. Because they all come to us to try to be acquired."

AI can now help turn a published fix into a working exploit in hours. Patching still takes weeks, and for many old routers, cameras, and supermarket fridges, a fix never arrives.

"So the question isn't how to patch faster. It's how to stop needing to."

Six openings for new cybersecurity companies today, each one making patching "unnecessary, or someone else's job":

1. Live fixes: blocks an exploit on running systems within hours, then has AI write and ship the real code fix

2. An AI first responder: spots attacks without hand-written rules and contains them as they unfold

3. Per-request access: checks every request from a person or their AI agents, with credentials that expire in minutes

4. Proven recovery: keeps restoring your backups in a sealed-off test environment to prove they work, with records insurers will accept

5. An install gateway: holds and sandboxes every package, extension and AI agent tool before it can run

6. Security for the long tail: one managed service for water utilities, clinics and others that will never have a security team

Full piece from a16z's Asaf Ezra and Steph Zhang: https://t.co/y6LXgU1fbi

John Somorjai of Salesforce on what kills company acquisition deals, from attrition hiding behind ARR to a veto from the security team:

"It's really important that you're ready and you're organized so that the data is flowing and it doesn't look like you're having trouble getting access to data."

"One of the mistakes that a lot of founders are making these days is they focus on one metric alone, which is ARR. And ARR is a wonderful metric, but it masks attrition."

"When you meet with a company that has very high attrition, that usually means that there are a lot of not just unhappy customers, but there might be some product quality issues as well."

"We have 14 functions that we work with on all of our diligence processes, and security is the one function that can hold up the red flag and say, 'I'm killing this deal.'"

"You definitely want to identify the vulnerabilities before we do."

"Nothing goes better in a process when a company is totally buttoned up... But when they don't, that's when, you know, deals can die."

His playbook is finding great technology that's starved for distribution and plugging it into 15,000 sales reps. Salesforce piloted Fin on its own help site, where it went live in 14 days and now handles over 40% of the traffic, resolving 65% without a human.

John joins a16z's Alex Immerman to discuss why Slack revenue is up almost 3x since the acquisition, how strong revenue can hide the churn that kills deals, the pen test that got into a CEO's laptop, and why robotics is where he's most excited to invest.

0:58 How Marc Benioff spots what to buy
3:48 The 3 tests for every acquisition
5:17 Salesforce's model as AI cuts seats
8:23 Fin resolves 65% with no human
10:32 The power of 15,000 sales reps
14:22 Founders who became product chiefs
17:34 Build vs buy when code is cheap
20:27 Why Salesforce bought Fin
22:58 Why Slack is perfect for AI agents
28:19 Salesforce Ventures' robotics bets
35:46 Why he's wary of new CRM startups
37:53 Why $10B+ startups have few buyers
39:32 Why he backed Anthropic six times
41:50 Red flags that kill acquisitions
44:27 The pen test that sank a deal
46:01 Growing up with a scientist father

YouTube: https://t.co/KQw7RiARu9

Be patient and keep stacking.

tweets.text:
Power costs have turned the AI build into a political fight.

Data centers used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and could need close to 12% by 2030. 

Keeping up means new plants and transmission lines that households help pay for through their power bills while the profit stays with the tech companies.

Households have been pushing back for more than a year, starting in 2025 when New Jersey and Virginia elected governors who campaigned on electricity costs. 

We flagged this in October as one of the signals to watch for the AI build.

This week the pushback reached the midterms. Voters sided against data centers in nearly every local ballot measure and elected governors who mostly back tighter rules on them. 

The Philadelphia chip index fell 12% two days later as markets sold off the biggest construction story they’ve had in decades.

Voters now help decide who pays for AI’s power and how fast the build can move.

thread_tweets.text:
🚨 October Jobs Report — Key Standouts (ASKB)

This morning’s BLS release for October was a significant upside surprise across the board.

HEADLINE NUMBERS

• Nonfarm Payrolls: +165,000 vs. ~65,000–70,000 expected
• Unemployment Rate: 4.1% vs. 4.2% expected
• Avg. Hourly Earnings: +0.4% MoM vs. +0.3% expected
• Avg. Hourly Earnings: +3.1% YoY vs. +2.9% expected
• Prior-month payrolls: +29,000, revised higher
KEY STANDOUTS
📈 Massive payroll beat
The +165,000 payroll print topped every economist forecast in the Bloomberg survey, which had a median estimate of roughly +70,000.
The result was also more than double the prior month’s revised +29,000 gain.

📉 Unemployment rate declined

The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, versus expectations for it to remain at 4.2%.

That adds to the picture of a labor market that remains considerably stronger than expected.

💵 Wages came in hot

Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.1% year-over-year.

Both were above consensus expectations, another potentially important signal for the Fed as it weighs the persistence of inflation pressures.

🔄 Prior months revised higher

The report also included upward revisions to the prior two months, making the overall picture stronger than the headline October gain alone would suggest.

🏭 Job gains were relatively broad-based

The strength was not concentrated in one industry.

On a 3-month moving-average basis, payroll growth has now accelerated to +137k, up from just +28k in July.

The latest 3-month sector breakdown shows:

• Education & Health Services: +37k
• Professional & Business Services: +36k
• Trade, Transportation & Utilities: +22k
• Manufacturing: +18k
• Leisure & Hospitality: +14k
• Government: +11k
• Construction: +10k
• Other Services: +5k
• Mining & Logging: ~0k
• Financial Activities: -4k
• Information: -11k

That is a notable broadening from earlier in the year, when employment growth was much weaker and more concentrated in a smaller number of sectors.

FED IMPLICATIONS

The combination of:

• stronger-than-expected payroll growth
• a lower unemployment rate
• hotter-than-expected wage growth
• upward revisions to prior months
• and broader sector participation
gives the Fed considerably less reason to worry about the labor side of its mandate.
Instead, the report likely keeps attention firmly focused on inflation and raises the bar for any near-term easing.
That said, one Bloomberg analysis cautioned that the strength could still prove to be something of a “head fake” given broader macro headwinds, including tariffs and elevated prices.
For now, though, the October jobs report is difficult to characterize as anything other than a significant upside surprise.

The +165,000 payroll print topped every economist forecast in the Bloomberg survey, which had a median estimate of roughly +70,000.
The result was also more than double the prior month’s revised +29,000 gain.

📉 Unemployment rate declined

The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, versus expectations for it to remain at 4.2%.

That adds to the picture of a labor market that remains considerably stronger than expected.

💵 Wages came in hot

Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.1% year-over-year.

Both were above consensus expectations, another potentially important signal for the Fed as it weighs the persistence of inflation pressures.

🔄 Prior months revised higher

The report also included upward revisions to the prior two months, making the overall picture stronger than the headline October gain alone would suggest.

🏭 Job gains were relatively broad-based

The strength was not concentrated in one industry.

On a 3-month moving-average basis, payroll growth has now accelerated to +137k, up from just +28k in July.

The latest 3-month sector breakdown shows:

• Education & Health Services: +37k
• Professional & Business Services: +36k
• Trade, Transportation & Utilities: +22k
• Manufacturing: +18k
• Leisure & Hospitality: +14k
• Government: +11k
• Construction: +10k
• Other Services: +5k
• Mining & Logging: ~0k
• Financial Activities: -4k
• Information: -11k

That is a notable broadening from earlier in the year, when employment growth was much weaker and more concentrated in a smaller number of sectors.

FED IMPLICATIONS

The combination of:

• stronger-than-expected payroll growth
• a lower unemployment rate
• hotter-than-expected wage growth
• upward revisions to prior months
• and broader sector participation
gives the Fed considerably less reason to worry about the labor side of its mandate.
Instead, the report likely keeps attention firmly focused on inflation and raises the bar for any near-term easing.
That said, one Bloomberg analysis cautioned that the strength could still prove to be something of a “head fake” given broader macro headwinds, including tariffs and elevated prices.
For now, though, the October jobs report is difficult to characterize as anything other than a significant upside surprise.

Markets just had an ugly week. A longer business cycle quietly turned favorable in the middle of it.

The Kitchin cycle, a roughly 3 to 5 year inventory cycle, entered a new favorable phase on October 31 that runs through May 2028. Since 1900, stocks have risen through these favorable stretches 89% of the time, with a median gain of 30.8%. Gains of 20% or more have outnumbered losses of that size 23 to 1.

This week's TradingEdge Weekly video covers the Kitchin cycle turn, a Nasdaq pattern match pointing to a choppy repair, breadth warnings stacking up, and gold at a one year low.

tweets.text:
Citrini's "State of the Themes" article kinda strengthens the Onchain/Decentralized AI thesis
 
The article argued that the AI infra/semis trades are ending because Neoclouds/Hyperscalers CAPEX is hitting ~$1T while AI eco ARR is only $200B and the huge gap won't be filled any time soon. Plus, financing constraints, construction delays and model price competition add pressure to the trade
 
That creates an interesting setup for projects helping operators monetize existing capacity and buyers access cheaper compute.
 
This is where Onchain/Decentralized AI gets interesting
 
1. Turning idle/crowdsourced GPUs into revenue
 
GPU marketplaces like @lium_io help operators rent out unused capacity, connecting existing hardware with paying customers.
 
For data centers and smaller operators, better utilization means more revenue from assets they’ve already paid for. Buyers get more options and competitive pricing (e.g. rent idle B200s on @lium_io for $4.25/hr).
 
As financing gets tighter, making existing hardware earn more becomes increasingly valuable.
 
2. Building markets for surplus/excess inference
 
Inference Providers and AI gateways have inference capacity they can sell. Some are expirables because they run subsidy campaigns but they couldn't get users to fully use them.
 
@AskSurplus connects these participants through an inference marketplace, routing requests across discounted supply. Selected offers carry discounts of 50–99% relative to listed API prices.
 
This creates a way for sellers to monetize unused allocations and buyers to reduce their inference bills.
 
Onchain settlement and tokenized credits add building blocks for developers to create new markets, routing tools and products around that supply.
 
3. Bootstrapping inference networks with existing GPUs
 
Decentralized AI crowdsources idle GPUs across the world.
 
Token emissions are used to pay for compute & inference instead of debt & equity financing huge CAPEX for data center buildouts.
 
Teams like @engyai and @dphnAI are already proving that it's possible to host top open-weight models on a hybrid/fully decentralized network that's fast, reliable, and cheap for users.
 
The opportunity is to turn fragmented hardware into useful, competitively priced inference.
 
The economics become stronger as paying customer demand grows enough to support suppliers with progressively smaller subsidies.
 
4. Expanding access to GPU financing
 
@USDai_Official connects onchain capital with operators financing GPU infrastructure.
 
That gives smaller operators another route to funding hardware purchases and deployments, with loans secured by GPUs and supported by their cash flows.
 
As traditional financing becomes more selective, access to additional capital sources could become increasingly valuable.
 
5. Making inference access a tradable asset
 
Pilots of inference tokenization are happening onchain first
 
@AskVenice tokenized its platform credits into "DIEM", people are buying & selling inference like a commodity and builders are building on top of it, creating venues where users can speculate & earn from their credits.
 
This creates the market for future inference access. Users can acquire capacity, trade the token representing that access, and earn revenue from it (if they don't use it).
 
Other teams are experimenting with similar models, creating more ways to price, distribute and monetize inference.
 
For tokens, this creates a link with extraneous demand outside of crypto. The more people use the platform, the more valuable the credits, the more valuable the token.
 
The investment case gets stronger when usage translates into value for token holders
 
The best part is that this sector is growing fast and teams are starting to align interest with token holders through buybacks & burn, revenue distribution, and more utilities.
 
Onchain/Decentralized AI provides the opportunities for better GPU utilization, cheaper inference, new financing channels and tradable access to compute/inference.
 
All real economic problems that crypto teams are building products around them.
 
2025-26 is the year of AI infra/semiconductors
 
2027 will be the year of Onchain/Decentralized AI

tweets.text:
Putting this in context.

2000: margin debt growth peaked Jan, S&P topped Mar, growth went negative May. Signal came after the top.
2007: growth peaked Jun, went negative Aug, S&P topped Oct. Signal came ~2 months before.
2021: growth peaked Jan, negative Jul, S&P topped Jan 2022. ~5 months early.

Now: growth peaked at +129% in June, went negative in Sep, and the S&P made its high on Oct 6. That's tracking closest to 2007.

But the index is only 1.7% off the high and still above its 10 month trend (~7,300). In every case the damage came once the trend broke, not when the signal fired. So this is the warning. The break hasn't happened yet.
